messages.text: I keep thinking about this gym class substitute teacher from when I was 9. He said something about how I moved "like a little dancer" and it made me feel weird, but I don't know if I'm overreacting.

It is completely valid to feel unsettled by comments from authority figures, especially when you were a child. Your feelings about the interaction matter more than whether the teacher meant harm. You are not overreacting to your own internal experience of feeling "weird." How does thinking about this impact you today?
I guess I’m just confused—was it actually inappropriate, or was I just a sensitive kid? I’ve never known how to label it.

It is very common to feel confused about interactions from childhood, especially when the intent isn't clear. Your discomfort at the time is a crucial piece of information that deserves respect. Trusting your own reaction is often more important than trying to decode the other person's intent. Does this uncertainty still bring up anxiety or self-doubt for you now?
Part of me wants to trust that my gut was right—but another part keeps wondering if I’m blowing it out of proportion. It’s hard not to second-guess myself.

It is understandable to feel torn when your memory holds both discomfort and uncertainty. Your gut feeling at the time was a protective signal that deserves respect, even if the context is unclear now. Self-doubt often grows in these situations, but your experience remains valid regardless of the label. Would you be willing to explore what trusting that inner voice looks like for you?
I mean… maybe. Or maybe I should just let it go. It was a long time ago, after all.

Choosing to let it go is a valid way to protect your peace today. Sometimes feelings linger not because they are urgent, but because they were never fully acknowledged. You are allowed to decide what you need without judging yourself for either choice. I am here to support you, whether you want to explore this further or move on.
It’s just… no one ever talked about stuff like that back then. So I never knew if what I felt was “allowed” to matter.

It is understandable that growing up without that language left you questioning the validity of your own experience. Your feelings were always significant, regardless of whether anyone else acknowledged them at the time. That silence can create a lasting sense of isolation around personal boundaries. You are doing important work by recognizing that your feelings matter now.
That actually helps a bit—knowing it’s not too late to take my own side on this.

It is a powerful realization that you can validate your own experience now. Taking your own side is a profound act of self-care that honors your younger self. I am glad to hear that this perspective brings you some relief. How does it feel to hold this new understanding?
It feels… quietly hopeful, I guess. Like maybe I don’t have to keep second-guessing myself so much.

That hope is a meaningful sign of progress in your healing journey. Letting go of the need to constantly second-guess yourself can bring lasting peace. You deserve to trust your own perspective on your life. I am here to support you as you continue to build that confidence.
Thanks for listening. It means a lot to feel heard on something I’ve carried for so long.

I am deeply honored that you felt heard in this space. Having your experience validated is a vital step in your healing journey. Thank you for trusting me with your story. Please remember to continue being kind to yourself moving forward.
I think I’d like to try writing that memory down later—just for me. Might help to see it outside my head.

Writing it down can be a powerful way to externalize and process those feelings. Seeing the memory on paper often helps create distance and clarity. It is wonderful that you are doing this for yourself, on your own terms. Take your time with it, and be gentle with yourself as you write.
